#9747. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9746. Initialize Once, Hydrate Deliberately: Choosing a FeatureCell's Starting State

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at sdux-vault.com

A FeatureCell does not start with "whatever was in the constructor." Calling initialize() activates the runtime pipeline, and the value it begins with depends on a resolved decision between a declared default, a previously persisted value, and a deliberate hydrate() factory. Knowing which source wins — and why — is what separates an accidental starting value from an intentional one.

This post walks through what initialize() actually activates, when hydrate() overrides everything else, and how to choose between a static default, Persist behaviors, and an explicit factory when your FeatureCell comes online.

Key takeaway: Initialization is not a direct mutation. Whatever value is selected — hydrated, persisted, or declared — is enqueued as a replaceState operation and processed through the same pipeline as any other update.

A FeatureCell is not operational the moment it is declared. It becomes a runtime participant only after initialize() is called — once, and exactly once. Reading state, issuing updates, or interacting with a FeatureCell before initialization results in a runtime error, and calling initialize() a second time does the same.

That boundary matters because initialization is where configuration becomes behavior. Filters, reducers, taps, error handlers, and emit configuration all have to be declared on the fluent builder before initialize() runs. Once initialization completes, the pipeline is fixed for the lifetime of that FeatureCell.

Calling initialize() transitions a FeatureCell from a configured definition into an active runtime participant. In order, it validates the declared configuration and behaviors, registers the FeatureCell with the Vault runtime, activates the Conductor execution surface, evaluates whichever initialization source was declared, and — if that source produced a value — enqueues it as the first replaceState operation.

If no initialization mechanism is declared at all, the FeatureCell still becomes active, but with value: undefined, waiting for an explicit replaceState() call. Declaring a default is optional; becoming active is not.

Here, descriptor.initialState is the only declared source, so that array becomes the first candidate through Resolve, Filters, Reducers, and Emit — the same pipeline any later update travels through.

During initialization, Vault evaluates exactly one initialization source, in strict precedence order:

These are not fallback layers. Vault does not try hydrate(), fail, and then fall back to Persist or the descriptor. Only the single highest-precedence declared source is evaluated at all.

hydrate(factory) registers a deferred factory that does not run when it is called — it runs only when initialize() runs. The factory may return a value synchronously, return a Promise, resolve to undefined, or throw. When declared, it overrides both Persist behaviors and descriptor.initialState outright, because declaring hydrate() is an explicit statement that persisted or static data should not be treated as authoritative for this initialization cycle.

⚠️ Warning: That descriptor still declares initialState: [], but once hydrate() is registered, it is never evaluated. Declaring both is not a layering strategy — only one source wins.

The practical question at startup is simple: should this FeatureCell begin with a declared default, a persisted value, or an explicit factory? Each source answers a different need.

Persisted storage can go stale the moment the underlying data changes elsewhere, and a static descriptor is static by definition. hydrate() exists for the case where neither of those should be treated as authoritative — if dynamic resolution is not actually needed, do not declare it, and Vault evaluates storage or the descriptor according to precedence instead.

A deferred factory does not always resolve the way you expect, and hydrate() treats "no value" very differently from "something went wrong."

An undefined result is not treated as a failure — it just means nothing committed. A thrown error or rejected Promise is treated as a failure, because the declared authoritative source did not resolve the way the application promised it would.

If that fetch rejects, initialization fails: hasValue stays false, value stays undefined, and error is populated. The pipeline keeps running — it does not crash the application — but nothing committed as declared. Recovery, if you want it, has to be explicit, using reset() and replaceState() to put the FeatureCell into a known state on your own terms.

⚠️ Warning: If hydrate() throws, Vault does not quietly drop down to Persist behaviors or descriptor.initialState. The FeatureCell does not activate partially, and the failure is visible instead of masked.

A live, interactive StackBlitz demo of hydrate() overriding a descriptor default is available on the original article if you want to try the sequence yourself.

Read the full method contracts for initialize() and hydrate() in the FeatureCell API reference, including the full precedence rules, diagrams, and resolution outcome tables this post draws from.

#9745. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9743. Node.js Compresses AI-Generated Images for Cloud Upload: Replaying Tenant Retention

For a game studio storing AI-generated training images, the difficult question is not how to upload bytes. It is how to prove, six months later, why an artifact still exists, which tenant owns it, and which retention rule produced that outcome.

Short answer: compress the image with Sharp, derive the object key from validated tenant and job identifiers, keep the object private, and persist the policy version beside the upload record. Replaying the same policy inputs should produce the same retention decision. The storage API is replaceable; that record is the governance boundary.

Infrai is a practical fit when this worker needs one REST API and one credential across backend capabilities, without installing a storage SDK. The upload contract can stay stable while the supported storage vendor behind it changes.

The before-and-after model is simple. Before, a cleanup task sees renders/final.webp and guesses. After, it sees tenant_42/training/2026-10/policy-3/job_8f2/image.webp, plus a record saying which policy version created it. The path is not an access-control system, but it makes an accidental cross-tenant reference much easier to detect.

Start with inputs, not a deletion date. For each generated image, store the tenant ID, training job ID, policy version, retention duration, object key, output format, byte count, and creation timestamp. Store the decision status too: eligible, held, or deleted. A worker can then recompute eligibility without inspecting pixels or relying on a mutable filename.

This is a useful distinction. A lifecycle rule is an execution mechanism. The policy record is the explanation.

Use a deterministic key convention, but do not treat it as a substitute for authorization. Validate tenant and job identifiers before interpolating them. Keep the bucket name configured by the deployment, not supplied by an end user. A private object and a signed URL for a reviewer preserve a much narrower access boundary than a permanent public link.

I initially treated compression as a storage concern only. That misses the operational part. A 12 MB source that becomes a 900 KB WebP is faster to retry, cheaper to move through a worker, and less burdensome for a later review tool. The byte count belongs in the policy record because it describes the workload that the retention process actually handled.

The example below keeps the image transformation and the write in one worker function. It uses an explicit PUT, a tenant-scoped key, a private ACL header, and an idempotency key derived from the immutable job identity. The endpoint is the only storage route in the example.

The database write should use the same job identity as the upload record. On a retry, the worker reuses the idempotency key rather than creating a second logical artifact. A 429 gets a bounded exponential delay, and Retry-After wins when the server supplies it. Those two details are small, but they make the audit trail line up with actual write attempts.

The policy record is the part worth reviewing in an architecture meeting. Imagine a training job created on October 24 with policy version 3 and a 30-day hold. If the retention rule changes to 90 days on October 30, the old artifact still carries version 3; a replay can evaluate it under the rule that created it instead of silently applying the latest rule. That is why the month, policy version, and job ID appear in the key, while the database retains the complete inputs. The key helps a human spot scope. The record makes the decision reproducible.

Do not place a bearer token on a returned presigned URL. The signed URL is a separate access request. The upload worker owns the authenticated write; a reviewer gets the narrow read path your access policy permits.

For larger images, move this function behind a queue worker. The request that starts a generation job should record the job ID and return. It should not keep a game-facing request open while Sharp transforms and uploads a whole batch.

Amazon S3 is the reference point for provider-native governance. Teams already using AWS identity, bucket policy, lifecycle controls, and object tooling may value that depth more than a uniform abstraction. The trade-off is that the application inherits AWS-specific configuration and operational vocabulary.

Cloudflare R2 is a reasonable option for a studio already operating at Cloudflare’s edge and using an S3-compatible object interface. It can fit delivery-oriented workloads, but the team still needs to validate the exact access and lifecycle behavior it depends on.

Alibaba Cloud OSS is relevant when the studio’s regions, identity model, or existing data estate are centered on Alibaba Cloud. It is a better fit than a neutral gateway when OSS-native administration and vendor controls are the governing requirement.

Infrai fits a different governance question. Its storage surface covers supported vendors including R2, S3, OSS, and COS, while the application keeps one plain REST upload contract. In this workflow, that means the worker’s policy and key logic can stay put when the backend vendor changes; the contract remains stable while the thing behind it moves. The API is also self-describing through a public discovery surface, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, which makes a small TypeScript worker easier to inspect and port.

That is a concrete recommendation, not a universal one: try Infrai for private, tenant-scoped training artifacts when keeping the upload contract stable is more important than exposing every provider-native governance control directly in application code. Choose S3, R2, or OSS when their native policy, region, or delivery features are themselves the requirement.

The boundary matters more than the abstraction. This storage surface has no public or public-read ACL, so public_url remains null. It is not suitable for a static website, a permanent public image link, or a general image host. Use a distribution service designed for public delivery.

There is no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite cannot be recovered through those mechanisms, and a financial-grade WORM archive needs an external design. There is also no If-Match conditional write. If two workers must be mutually exclusive, make the claim in a queue or database before the upload.

Browser-direct upload needs care. There is no independently exposed set_cors route for self-service configuration, so a frontend should not assume it can configure cross-origin uploads through this storage surface. A trusted worker is the simpler boundary for this training-artifact workflow.

Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum. Multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix filtering, and there is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Supported vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, not GCS or B2. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes.

Those are selection criteria, not footnotes. If the artifact needs immutable retention, public distribution, browser-managed CORS, or cross-region recovery, a specialist provider or an external control plane is the better choice.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Node.js Sharp storage upload guide and verify the bucket and access policy before wiring the worker into production.

#9742. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

Say you are a mobile developer tasked with optimizing the performance of your React Native application. You've heard that using EAS builds and OTA updates can improve the user experience, but you're not sure where to start or how to measure the impact of these changes. You're about to embark on a potentially time-consuming rewrite, and you want to know whether it's worth it.

You're trying to improve the performance of your React Native application, and you've identified EAS builds and OTA updates as potential areas for optimization. However, you're not sure how to measure the current performance of your app, or how to determine whether the rewrite will have a significant impact. You've tried using various metrics, such as app launch time and battery usage, but you're not sure which ones are most relevant or how to collect accurate data.

EAS builds and OTA updates can have a significant impact on the performance of a React Native application, but measuring this impact can be challenging. One of the main reasons is that there are many factors that can affect performance, such as network connectivity, device hardware, and user behavior. Additionally, the metrics that are typically used to measure performance, such as app launch time and battery usage, may not be directly related to the changes made during the rewrite. To make matters worse, the documentation for EAS builds and OTA updates often focuses on the features and functionality, rather than the performance implications.

#9739. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9738. Sparen of beleggen: waar groeit je geld het hardst?

Bij ons thuis werd sparen vroeger besproken alsof het een deugd was — en beleggen alsof het een gok was. Mijn ouders hadden hun geld op een spaarrekening, punt. Dat stond veilig, dat kon je zien groeien, en daar sliep je goed van. Ik heb dat lang klakkeloos overgenomen, tot ik een keer naast elkaar uitrekende wat honderd euro per maand doet op een spaarrekening versus in een gespreide belegging. Het verschil was zo groot dat ik mijn ouders er bijna over belde. Bijna — want het eerlijke verhaal is genuanceerder dan "beleggen wint". Laten we het goed uitrekenen, met de voor- én nadelen erbij.

Eerst het sparen. Je zet €100 per maand op een rekening met 2% rente, maandelijks bijgeschreven. Na twintig jaar staat er €29.529 — zelf heb je €24.000 ingelegd, dus de rente heeft er zo'n €5.529 bij gedaan. Dat is precies wat sparen belooft: voorspelbaar, rustig, en je geld is er als je het nodig hebt. Er valt geen maand tussen waarin je saldo ineens tien procent lager staat. Voor geld dat je binnen nu en een paar jaar nodig hebt — een auto, een aanbetaling, een buffer — is dat niet alleen verstandig, dat is de enige juiste keuze.

Dan het beleggen, met dezelfde honderd euro per maand. Tegen 5% gemiddeld rendement heb je na twintig jaar €41.275. Tegen 7% is het €52.397. Zelfde inleg van €24.000, maar het rendement is dan respectievelijk €17.275 of €28.397 — tegenover die €5.529 van de spaarrekening. En hoe langer je het laat staan, hoe schever de verhouding wordt. Na dertig jaar: sparen tegen 2% geeft €49.355 van je €36.000 inleg, terwijl 7% uitkomt op €122.709. Meer dan twee keer zoveel eindkapitaal uit exact hetzelfde maandbedrag. De regel van 72 verklaart waarom: deel 72 door je rendement en je hebt de verdubbelingstijd. Bij 2% duurt verdubbelen zo'n 36 jaar, bij 7% ongeveer 10 jaar. De belegger ziet zijn geld in dezelfde periode dus ruim drie keer verdubbelen waar de spaarder nog op zijn eerste verdubbeling wacht.

Er is nog een onzichtbare tegenstander die vooral spaarders raakt: inflatie. Geld dat stilstaat, verliest koopkracht. Reken maar mee: €100.000 dat dertig jaar blijft liggen, is bij 2% inflatie in koopkracht van nu nog maar ongeveer €55.000 waard. Je saldo lijkt gelijk, maar je kunt er bijna de helft minder mee kopen. Bij een spaarrente van 2% en inflatie van 2% ren je dus op een loopband: je cijfer groeit, je werkelijke vermogen niet. Dat betekent niet dat sparen zinloos is — het betekent dat sparen een ander doel dient dan groeien.

Want nu de eerlijke keerzijde van beleggen, want die hoort er net zo hard bij. Die 5% en 7% zijn gemiddelden over lange perioden, geen jaarlijkse beloftes. Er komen jaren met min tien of min twintig procent, en niemand weet wanneer. Wie dan in paniek verkoopt, maakt van een tijdelijke dip een definitief verlies. Beleggen vraagt dus twee dingen: een horizon van minstens tien jaar, en het temperament om onderweg niet aan de knoppen te zitten. Kun je een van beide niet opbrengen, dan is het hogere eindbedrag in de tabel voor jou een fictief getal.

Mijn eigen antwoord is daarom geen óf-óf maar een verdeling. Het geld dat ik binnen enkele jaren nodig heb, plus een buffer van een paar maanden vaste lasten voor noodgevallen, staat op de spaarrekening — daar hoort het veilig en direct beschikbaar te zijn. Alles daarboven, geld dat ik tien jaar of langer kan missen, beleg ik gespreid en saai. Zo hoef ik me bij een beursdaling nooit zorgen te maken over de huur, en hoeft mijn verre-toekomstgeld niet weg te kwijnen onder de inflatie. Sparen en beleggen zijn geen concurrenten; ze doen gewoon elk een andere baan.

Waar je geld het hardst groeit, is wiskundig dus duidelijk. Waar het bij jou het beste staat, hangt af van wanneer je het nodig hebt. Wil je je eigen situatie doorrekenen — je eigen maandbedrag, een eigen mix van percentages en looptijden — dan kun je zelf rente op rente berekenen met de gratis calculator van Toolkistje en de scenario's naast elkaar zetten. Reken het een keer uit voor je buffer én voor je lange termijn, en de verdeling maakt zichzelf bijna vanzelf.

#9737. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9736. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9735. RevOps Is Quietly Becoming an Engineering Job

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Over the last two weeks, I've written here about a calendar table that knows November 1 has 25 hours, a customer health score that barely beats a coin flip, a 1961 warehouse formula that finds dead deals in a CRM, a Slack report that checks its own numbers before it posts, an exam for AI agents, a macOS job that died because of where it kept its log file, and why 3x pipeline coverage is a guess.

My title is Head of Revenue Operations. Very little of that shows up in a RevOps job description.

I started in supply chain, moved into revenue operations, and taught myself SQL along the way. For most of that time, the job looked the way people describe it: own the CRM, build the reports, run the forecast, keep sales and finance looking at the same numbers. That's still the job. But the way it gets done has changed, and I think it's changing faster than the job descriptions.

The data moved into the warehouse. RevOps used to live inside the CRM and its report builder. Now the numbers that matter, from billing, product usage, payments, and the CRM itself, land in Snowflake or BigQuery. The person who reconciles them needs SQL, not a report wizard.

Writing code got cheap. An AI coding agent will write the script that syncs the CRM, builds the workbook, or posts the report in minutes. That's the real shift. When code is cheap, more of RevOps becomes code, and someone has to run it.

Running it is the part that didn't get cheaper. A script is easy. A script that runs at 7:45 every morning for two years, survives a laptop update, posts nothing when the data is wrong, and tells someone when it didn't run at all: that's operations engineering. And it's increasingly a RevOps problem, because the scripts are about revenue and nobody else owns them.

If you work in RevOps, sales ops, or finance ops and you're wondering where to invest, here's my list, roughly in order of how often each one has saved me.

SQL, properly. Not just SELECT and GROUP BY. Grain, joins that duplicate rows, window functions, time zones. Most wrong numbers I've chased came down to a join or a day boundary. (These six Snowflake patterns cover the ones I reach for every week.)

One scheduler, and how it fails. cron, launchd, GitHub Actions, Airflow. Pick the one you'll actually use and learn what it does when things go wrong. Every scheduler has a way to fail silently. Know yours.

Version control for anything that produces a number. If it ends up in front of a CFO, it goes in git. "Which version of the query made that slide?" should have an answer.

Testing numbers, not just code. Reconciliations, check cells, golden questions with known answers. Code that runs is not code that's right.

Staging and promotion. Somewhere to break things that isn't production, and a deliberate step between the two.

Writing definitions down. Every metric needs a written definition that sales and finance have both agreed to. It's the least technical item on this list, and the one that prevents the most arguments.

Working with AI agents. Give them a sandbox, an exam, and a short list of things they're never allowed to touch. Then let them do a lot of the typing.

The risk in all of this is that RevOps turns into a shadow data engineering team: pipelines nobody else understands, a dozen scheduled jobs on one laptop, and a single person who knows how any of it works. That version is worse than not automating at all.

So draw a line. Data engineering owns the platform: ingestion, the warehouse, the infrastructure everyone shares. RevOps owns the business logic and the last mile: the definitions, the reconciliations, the reports, and the small automations that move revenue numbers to the people who use them.

And give the last mile an exit. When a RevOps automation becomes important enough that its failure would hurt the company, it graduates to the platform, with real monitoring, an owner on call, and a second person who understands it.

Most RevOps postings still ask for CRM administration, reporting, and strong analytical skills. Those matter. But the people I see doing this job well now are also comfortable in a terminal, can read a stack trace without panic, and treat a scheduled job like a product with users.

The title still says operations. More and more, the work says engineering. The people who do well will be the ones who take both words seriously.

The pieces mentioned at the top, with runnable code, are on my HackerNoon profile.

I'm Malek Damiri, head of revenue operations in Atlanta. I write about revenue operations and the systems behind it at malekdamiri.com.

#9734. Measuring the Impact of Expo Router Deep Links

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at amitchakraborty.dev

Say you are a mobile app developer working on a React Native project using Expo Router. You've heard about the benefits of deep links, but you're not sure if implementing them will have a significant impact on your app's performance. You've tried to measure the effect of deep links on your app's routing, but you're not sure what metrics to track or how to instrument your app to get meaningful data.

You were trying to optimize your app's routing to improve user experience, but you're not sure if the effort will be worth it. You've seen a symptom - a noticeable delay when navigating between screens - but you don't know if it's related to deep links or something else. The delay is costing you users, who are abandoning your app due to frustration with its performance.

Expo Router deep links can improve app performance by allowing the app to navigate directly to a specific screen, rather than loading the entire app and then navigating to the desired screen. However, implementing deep links requires changes to your app's routing configuration, which can be complex and time-consuming. To determine whether the effort is worth it, you need to measure the impact of deep links on your app's performance.

One key metric to track is the time it takes for the app to navigate between screens. This can be measured using the navigation module in Expo Router, which provides a navigate function that returns a promise that resolves when the navigation is complete. You can use this promise to measure the time it takes for the navigation to complete, and compare it to the time it takes without deep links.

Implementing Expo Router deep links can require significant changes to your app's routing configuration, which can be time-consuming and may require additional testing. However, if your app has a complex routing hierarchy or requires frequent navigation between screens, the benefits of deep links may outweigh the costs.

When interviewing a candidate for a React Native developer position, you may ask a question like: "How would you measure the impact of Expo Router deep links on app performance?" A weak answer might focus on the benefits of deep links without discussing how to measure their impact. A strong answer would describe the instrumentation technique outlined above, including how to measure navigation time and compare it to the navigation time with deep links. The candidate should also be able to discuss the trade-offs between implementing deep links and other optimization techniques, and evaluate the impact of deep links on user engagement metrics. A follow-up question might ask the candidate to describe a scenario in which deep links would not be necessary, and how they would determine whether the benefits of deep links outweigh the costs.

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9731. The DevOps bootcamp · 4. Git as an operations tool

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at amitchakraborty.dev

The DevOps bootcamp · Chapter 4 of 14 · DevOps · new chapter every Thursday morning

By the end of this chapter: Use branches, tags and history the way a delivery pipeline reads them.

You are a junior engineer on your first backend project, and you need to test a branch on the team's shared staging server. You SSH into the server, pull your code, and run the start command. However, the terminal returns an error message: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::8080. This error indicates that another process is already using port 8080, which is the port your application is trying to use.

You try changing the port, but the proxy routing traffic to your application expects it to be running on port 8080. You assume the previous version of the application is still running, but you do not know how to find it. You try running your new application as the superuser to force it through, and it starts, but immediately crashes with Permission denied: /var/log/staging-api/error.log. This error message suggests that your application does not have the necessary permissions to write to the log file.

You have wasted an hour trying to troubleshoot the issue, and you are still no closer to testing your branch. You need to understand how to manage different versions of your application, how to find and stop running processes, and how to handle permissions issues.

To follow along with this chapter, you need to have Git installed on your machine, and you should have a basic understanding of Linux commands, such as navigating the file system and running processes. You should also have a Git repository set up for your project. You can verify that Git is installed by running the command git --version in your terminal. The output should display the version of Git installed on your machine, such as git version 2.37.1.

In Git, a branch is a separate line of development in your repository. You can think of it as a separate copy of your codebase that you can work on independently of the main codebase. When you create a new branch, Git creates a new pointer to the current commit, and any changes you make will be committed to that branch.

To create a new branch, you can use the command git branch . For example, to create a new branch called feature/new-feature, you would run the command git branch feature/new-feature. You can then switch to that branch using the command git checkout feature/new-feature.

Git tags are used to mark specific points in your repository's history. They are often used to mark releases or milestones. To create a new tag, you can use the command git tag . For example, to create a new tag called v1.0, you would run the command git tag v1.0.

Git history refers to the record of all changes made to your repository over time. You can view the history of your repository using the command git log. This will display a list of all commits made to your repository, including the commit message, author, and date.
